name: 7. Security and authentication
description: Auth flows, encryption, RBAC, MFA, audit logging, privacy.

cards.subject: Password hashing
says: turns a password into a fixed-size value that cannot be reversed to the password
lets a system check a password without storing it
cards.use: need to store user passwords safely
not: can be undone with the right key to recover the password

cards.subject: A salt
says: is a random value added to each password before hashing
makes identical passwords produce different hashes
defeats precomputed rainbow tables
cards.use: want two users with the same password to have different stored hashes
not: must be kept secret in the way an encryption key is

cards.subject: A pepper
says: is a secret value mixed into password hashes and kept outside the database
protects hashes when only the database leaks
cards.use: want a stolen database alone to be insufficient for cracking passwords
not: is stored beside the hash in the same row

cards.subject: Key stretching
says: makes every password guess deliberately expensive
uses a tunable work factor that can be raised over time
slows down offline brute force after a database leak
cards.use: want guessing millions of passwords a second to be impractical
not: makes the password itself longer for the user

cards.subject: A memory-hard hash
says: needs a large amount of memory for every guess
makes cracking on GPUs and custom hardware costlier
is exemplified by scrypt and Argon2
cards.use: choose an algorithm for storing new passwords
not: is a fast general-purpose digest suited to file checksums

cards.subject: Multi-factor authentication
says: requires a second kind of proof beyond the password
limits the damage when a password is stolen or guessed
cards.use: want a stolen password alone to be useless to an attacker
not: replaces the password completely

cards.subject: A passkey
says: uses a public and private key pair for each site
keeps the private key on the user's device
resists phishing because the credential is bound to the genuine site
cards.use: want sign-in that a fake login page cannot capture
not: is a longer password stored in a password manager

cards.subject: OAuth 2.0
says: lets an app obtain limited access to a resource on a user's behalf
issues access tokens so the user's password is never shared with the app
is fundamentally a delegated authorisation framework
cards.use: want a third-party app to read a user's calendar without their password
not: proves who the user is on its own

cards.subject: OpenID Connect
says: adds an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0
returns an ID token that describes who signed in
is the usual basis for single sign-on
cards.use: need single sign-on that tells the app who the user is
not: is an older replacement for TLS

cards.subject: PKCE
says: binds the authorisation code exchange to a secret the client created
stops an intercepted authorisation code being redeemed by an attacker
protects clients that cannot keep a client secret, such as mobile and single-page apps
cards.use: build a public client that cannot hold a secret
not: encrypts the access token while it sits in storage

cards.subject: A session token
says: identifies a signed-in browser on later requests
should be long, random and unguessable
must be treated like a password while it is valid
cards.use: need the server to recognise a user after login
not: can safely be a sequential number such as the user id

cards.subject: The HttpOnly cookie flag
says: hides the cookie from JavaScript
limits what an injected script can read directly
cards.use: want a cookie that page scripts cannot read
not: stops the cookie being sent over plain HTTP

cards.subject: The Secure cookie flag
says: tells the browser to send the cookie only over HTTPS
keeps the cookie off unencrypted connections
cards.use: want a cookie never sent over plain HTTP
not: hides the cookie from JavaScript

cards.subject: The SameSite cookie attribute
says: limits when the browser attaches a cookie to cross-site requests
reduces the risk of CSRF
has Lax and Strict modes with different strictness
cards.use: want to blunt cross-site request forgery with a cookie setting
not: encrypts the cookie value

cards.subject: Session fixation
says: happens when an attacker sets the session identifier before the victim signs in
is prevented by issuing a fresh identifier at login
cards.use: issue a new session identifier when a user authenticates
not: is stopped by making the session cookie HttpOnly

cards.subject: Server-side session revocation
says: lets the server invalidate a token before it expires
supports signing a user out of every device
relies on state the server keeps, such as a per-user version
cards.use: need to cut off a stolen session immediately
not: is unnecessary when the cookie has an expiry date

cards.subject: A JSON Web Token
says: is a signed token that carries claims
is verified by checking its signature and its claims
cannot be revoked before expiry without server-side state
cards.use: hand a signed set of claims between services
not: is encrypted by default so its payload is secret

cards.subject: Authentication
says: proves who a user is
happens before authorisation in a request
cards.use: need to confirm the identity of the caller
not: decides which records the caller may edit

cards.subject: Authorisation
says: decides what an identified user may do
is checked on the server for each sensitive action
cards.use: decide whether a signed-in user may delete a record
not: proves who the user is

cards.subject: Role-based access control
says: grants permissions through roles
assigns each user to a role such as learner, manager or admin
cards.use: want permissions managed per job function and not per person
not: decides using only the time of day and location

cards.subject: Attribute-based access control
says: decides using attributes of the user, the resource and the context
can express a rule such as same department and office hours only
cards.use: need rules that depend on the record and the situation, not only the role
not: is limited to a fixed list of roles

cards.subject: Least privilege
says: gives an account only the access its job needs
limits the damage when an account is compromised
cards.use: grant a new service account permissions
not: gives everyone admin rights to avoid support tickets

cards.subject: Deny by default
says: refuses every request that no rule explicitly allows
makes a forgotten rule fail safe
cards.use: design a new permission check
not: allows everything until a rule blocks it

cards.subject: An ownership check
says: confirms the record being accessed belongs to the caller
stops one user reading another's data by changing an id
cards.use: accept a record id from the request
not: is satisfied by checking that the user is signed in

cards.subject: Horizontal privilege escalation
says: gives a user access to another user's data at the same level
is what a missing ownership check allows
cards.use: see a user read a peer's record by editing an id
not: lets an ordinary user gain admin powers

cards.subject: Vertical privilege escalation
says: gives an ordinary user the abilities of a higher role
can happen when a role field is accepted from the request body
cards.use: see a learner reach an admin-only function
not: lets a user read a peer's record at the same role

cards.subject: Separation of duties
says: splits a sensitive task so no single person can complete it alone
reduces the risk of insider fraud
cards.use: stop one person both requesting and approving a payment
not: gives one trusted admin control of the whole process

cards.subject: SQL injection
says: lets attacker input change the structure of a database query
is reliably prevented by parameterised queries
cards.use: see user input joined into a query string
not: is fixed reliably by hiding database error messages

cards.subject: Command injection
says: passes untrusted input to an operating system shell
is avoided by not invoking a shell and by passing arguments as a list
cards.use: see user input placed inside a shell command
not: only affects databases

cards.subject: Cross-site scripting
says: runs attacker script in a victim's browser within the site's origin
is prevented mainly by context-aware output encoding
cards.use: see user input written into a page without encoding
not: is the same thing as CSRF

cards.subject: Stored XSS
says: saves the malicious script on the server so every viewer receives it
can hit users who never clicked a crafted link
cards.use: find a comment field that shows other users' text to all visitors
not: needs the victim to follow a crafted link each time

cards.subject: Reflected XSS
says: bounces a script from the request straight into the response
usually needs the victim to follow a crafted link
cards.use: see a search term echoed into the results page
not: persists in the database until it is removed

cards.subject: DOM-based XSS
says: arises when client-side code writes untrusted data into the page, such as through innerHTML
can occur even when the server response is clean
cards.use: see front-end code pass location.hash to innerHTML
not: always requires the server to store the payload

cards.subject: Cross-site request forgery
says: makes a victim's browser send an unwanted authenticated request
relies on the browser attaching cookies automatically
is mitigated by anti-forgery tokens and SameSite cookies
cards.use: worry that a malicious page could trigger a state-changing request on a logged-in site
not: lets the attacker read the victim's responses

cards.subject: Server-side request forgery
says: makes the server fetch a URL the attacker chose
can reach internal services and cloud metadata endpoints
is mitigated by allow-listing destinations
cards.use: build a feature that fetches a URL supplied by the user
not: runs script in the visitor's browser

cards.subject: Insecure direct object reference
says: exposes a record when changing an identifier in a request is not checked against the caller
is a form of broken access control
cards.use: find that changing /orders/41 to /orders/42 shows someone else's order
not: is prevented by making identifiers longer

cards.subject: Security misconfiguration
says: leaves defaults, debug modes or open services exposed
includes default credentials left unchanged
cards.use: find a debug console reachable in production
not: is always caused by a flaw in application code

cards.subject: Path traversal
says: uses sequences such as ../ to reach files outside the intended directory
is prevented by resolving the path and confirming it stays inside the base directory
cards.use: let a user name a file to download
not: lets the attacker run SQL

cards.subject: An open redirect
says: sends users to an attacker-chosen URL from a trusted domain
makes phishing links look genuine
cards.use: see a login page redirect to a next parameter without checking it
not: injects script into the page

cards.subject: Mass assignment
says: binds every request field onto an object, including ones the user should not set
can let a user set their own role
cards.use: see a framework create a record straight from the request body
not: is caused by weak password hashing

cards.subject: Account enumeration
says: reveals whether an account exists through different messages or response times
helps attackers target real users
cards.use: see login fail faster for unknown emails than for known ones
not: guesses the password of one account

cards.subject: A race condition
says: exploits the gap between a check and the action that relies on it
can let a one-use coupon be redeemed twice
cards.use: see two simultaneous requests both pass the same check
not: only occurs on single-threaded servers

cards.subject: A timing attack
says: infers a secret from how long an operation takes
is countered by constant-time comparison
cards.use: compare a secret token supplied by the caller
not: needs the attacker to read the server's memory

cards.subject: A parameterised query
says: sends the SQL and the data separately so data is never parsed as code
is the primary defence against SQL injection
cards.use: need to put user input into a database query
not: works by stripping the word SELECT from input

cards.subject: Output encoding
says: converts special characters so the browser treats data as text
must match the context, such as HTML body, attribute or JavaScript
cards.use: need to show user-supplied text in a page
not: is performed once on input and then trusted everywhere

cards.subject: Input validation
says: checks that incoming data matches the expected type, length and format
runs on the server, whatever the browser already checked
is a layer of defence and not a substitute for encoding
cards.use: receive a field from a form or API call
not: makes output encoding unnecessary

cards.subject: Allow-list validation
says: accepts only values known to be good
is safer than trying to list every bad input
cards.use: accept a sort column name that must be one of a few fields
not: rejects a few known bad strings and accepts the rest

cards.subject: A Content Security Policy
says: tells the browser which sources of script and content are allowed
limits the damage of an XSS bug
cards.use: want a second line of defence against injected script
not: replaces the need to encode output

cards.subject: HTTP Strict Transport Security
says: tells the browser to use only HTTPS for the site for a stated period
defeats downgrade and SSL-stripping attacks
cards.use: want browsers never to try plain HTTP for the site
not: blocks the page from being framed

cards.subject: Referrer-Policy
says: controls how much of the URL is sent in the Referer header
keeps sensitive URL details from leaking to other sites
cards.use: want to stop a link click leaking the current page's address
not: decides which sites may embed the page

cards.subject: The frame-ancestors directive
says: controls which sites may embed the page in a frame
defends against clickjacking
cards.use: want to stop the page being framed by another site
not: lists the origins that may run scripts

cards.subject: An anti-CSRF token
says: is an unpredictable value the server checks on state-changing requests
cannot be read by an attacker's cross-site page
cards.use: protect a form that changes data with cookie authentication
not: is the same as the session cookie

cards.subject: CORS
says: relaxes the browser's same-origin policy for named origins
is enforced by the browser and not by the server
does not stop non-browser clients from calling the API
cards.use: let a browser app on one origin read responses from an API on another
not: is an authentication mechanism

cards.subject: Generic error messages
says: show users a general failure while details go to server logs
avoid leaking stack traces and query text
cards.use: decide what an error page should reveal
not: help attackers by hiding the real cause from developers

cards.subject: A secrets manager
says: stores secrets centrally with access control and audit
can rotate secrets and hand out short-lived credentials
cards.use: want to keep credentials out of code and config files
not: is a public repository where teams share keys

cards.subject: Secret scanning
says: searches commits and files for leaked credentials
can run as a pre-commit hook and in the CI pipeline
cards.use: want to catch a committed key before it is pushed
not: encrypts any secret it finds

cards.subject: Key rotation
says: replaces a key on a schedule or after a suspected leak
limits how long a stolen key stays useful
cards.use: suspect a key may have been exposed
not: makes old data permanently unreadable

cards.subject: A secret committed to git
says: stays recoverable from history after a later commit deletes the file
must be revoked and replaced, not just removed
cards.use: discover a live key in an old commit
not: is fixed by deleting the file in the next commit

cards.subject: Short-lived credentials
says: expire automatically after minutes or hours
shrink the window in which a leaked value can be used
cards.use: want a leak to be harmless after a short time
not: never need to be rotated because they are permanent

cards.subject: Envelope encryption
says: encrypts data with a data key that is itself encrypted by a master key
lets the master key be rotated without re-encrypting all the data
cards.use: need to encrypt large volumes of data under a managed master key
not: uses one password to encrypt every file separately

cards.subject: Per-environment secrets
says: use different values in development, staging and production
stop a leaked development key opening production
cards.use: set up configuration for several deployment environments
not: share one production key with every developer laptop

cards.subject: A secret in a frontend bundle
says: is readable by every visitor
cannot be hidden by minification or obfuscation
cards.use: consider putting an API key in browser JavaScript
not: is safe because the source is compiled

cards.subject: Symmetric encryption
says: uses the same key to encrypt and decrypt
is fast enough for bulk data
cards.use: need to encrypt a large file quickly
not: uses a public key to encrypt and a private key to decrypt

cards.subject: Asymmetric encryption
says: uses a public and private key pair
lets strangers send protected data without a shared secret
cards.use: need two parties with no prior shared key to communicate securely
not: uses a single shared key for both directions

cards.subject: TLS
says: protects data in transit between client and server
authenticates the server with a certificate
provides confidentiality and integrity for the connection
cards.use: need to protect traffic between a browser and a site
not: encrypts data stored on the server's disk

cards.subject: Encryption at rest
says: protects stored data if disks or backups are stolen
does not stop an authorised application from reading the data
cards.use: worry about a stolen backup tape
not: protects data travelling across the network

cards.subject: A digital signature
says: proves who produced data and that it was not altered
is created with a private key and checked with the public key
cards.use: need to prove a release came from the publisher
not: is made with a shared secret known to both sides

cards.subject: An HMAC
says: authenticates a message using a shared secret key
lets the receiver detect tampering with the message
cards.use: need two services holding the same secret to verify each other's messages
not: can be verified by anyone holding only a public key

cards.subject: AES-GCM
says: is authenticated encryption giving confidentiality and integrity
needs a unique nonce for every encryption under one key
cards.use: want encryption that also detects tampering
not: is a hash algorithm used to store passwords

cards.subject: ECB mode
says: encrypts identical plaintext blocks to identical ciphertext blocks
leaks patterns in the data
cards.use: see a block cipher used with no IV or nonce
not: is the recommended mode for encrypting images

cards.subject: A cryptographically secure random generator
says: produces unpredictable values suitable for tokens and keys
should replace Math.random for anything secret
cards.use: generate a password reset token
not: is too slow to be used for session tokens

cards.subject: Base64
says: is a reversible encoding with no key
provides no confidentiality
cards.use: see a credential that looks scrambled but is only Base64
not: is a form of encryption

cards.subject: Rate limiting
says: caps how many requests a client may make in a time window
blunts password guessing and scraping
cards.use: want to slow repeated login attempts
not: permanently bans any visitor who fails once

cards.subject: Credential stuffing
says: replays username and password pairs leaked from other sites
succeeds because people reuse passwords
cards.use: see many logins succeed with valid pairs from a past breach elsewhere
not: tries every possible password for one account

cards.subject: Password spraying
says: tries a few common passwords across many accounts
avoids per-account lockout
cards.use: see one common password tried against every account
not: replays pairs leaked from another service

cards.subject: Account lockout
says: blocks sign-in after repeated failures
can itself be abused to lock real users out
cards.use: weigh stopping guessing against denying service to a user
not: has no downside for the legitimate user

cards.subject: X-Forwarded-For spoofing
says: lets a client fake its address when the app trusts the header blindly
defeats per-IP rate limits
cards.use: sit behind proxies and need the real client address
not: only affects the TLS handshake

cards.subject: A token bucket
says: allows short bursts up to a bucket size while enforcing an average rate
refills at a steady rate
cards.use: want a limiter that tolerates brief bursts but caps the average
not: resets its counter to zero at fixed clock boundaries

cards.subject: A web application firewall
says: filters HTTP requests against rules for known attack patterns
is a layer and not a substitute for fixing the code
cards.use: want a stopgap filter in front of a vulnerable app
not: makes input validation in the application unnecessary

cards.subject: An audit log
says: records who did what to which target and when
covers sensitive actions such as sign-ins, role changes and exports
cards.use: need to answer who changed this setting
not: is the same thing as debug output for developers

cards.subject: Append-only log storage
says: prevents past entries being edited or deleted
is kept apart from the system it records
cards.use: want an attacker unable to erase their trail
not: lets administrators tidy old entries freely

cards.subject: Sensitive data in logs
says: turns a log file into a credential leak
is avoided by redacting passwords and tokens before writing
cards.use: see a request body written to the log verbatim
not: is acceptable because logs are internal

cards.subject: Structured logging
says: writes events as key-value fields rather than free text
makes searching and alerting reliable
cards.use: want to query logs by user or action
not: is only useful for human reading

cards.subject: Security alerting
says: notifies a person when events cross a defined threshold
can fire on many failed sign-ins from one source
cards.use: want to learn about an attack while it is happening
not: replaces the need for logs

cards.subject: Log injection
says: forges log lines by placing newlines in untrusted input
is prevented by encoding input or using structured logging
cards.use: see user input written straight into a plain-text log line
not: gives the attacker a shell on the server

cards.subject: A known dependency vulnerability
says: is a published flaw in a library you include
is found by scanning against vulnerability databases
cards.use: learn that a library you use has a CVE
not: only matters for code you wrote yourself

cards.subject: A transitive dependency
says: is pulled in by a package you chose and not by you directly
can carry flaws that never appear in your manifest
cards.use: audit what a project really includes
not: is always listed explicitly in your own package file

cards.subject: A lockfile
says: pins exact dependency versions
gives repeatable builds across machines
cards.use: want every build to install the same versions
not: upgrades every dependency to the newest release automatically

cards.subject: A software bill of materials
says: lists the components and versions inside a build
lets you find affected products quickly when a flaw is announced
cards.use: need to know which products contain a newly disclosed vulnerable library
not: is a financial invoice for licences

cards.subject: Typosquatting
says: publishes a malicious package with a name close to a popular one
relies on a developer mistyping an install command
cards.use: see a package named almost like a well-known library
not: compromises the real maintainer's account

cards.subject: Dependency confusion
says: tricks a build into fetching a public package in place of an internal one with the same name
is reduced by scoped namespaces and pinning registries
cards.use: worry that a build might pull a public package named like a private one
not: relies on a typing mistake in the install command

cards.subject: Artifact signing
says: lets consumers verify an artifact came from the expected publisher
detects tampering after the build
cards.use: want users to confirm a release was not altered
not: encrypts the artifact so only the publisher can open it

cards.subject: Automated dependency updates
says: open pull requests for newer versions
make patching a routine and not a crisis
cards.use: want upgrades to arrive as small regular changes
not: merge every update without any tests

cards.subject: Threat modelling
says: identifies what can go wrong in a design before it is built
asks what are we building, what can go wrong and what will we do about it
cards.use: want to find design flaws before writing code
not: is carried out only after a penetration test finds a bug

cards.subject: A data flow diagram
says: shows processes, data stores, external entities and the flows between them
is the usual input to a STRIDE review
cards.use: need a picture to review a system for threats
not: lists every vulnerability found in a scan

cards.subject: A trust boundary
says: marks where data passes between different levels of trust
is where authentication and validation checks belong
cards.use: decide where to validate incoming data
not: is the outer wall of the office building

cards.subject: The attack surface
says: is the sum of the points where an attacker can try to get in or extract data
grows with each endpoint, feature and exposed service
cards.use: want to reduce what an attacker can reach by removing unused endpoints
not: is measured only by the number of lines of code

cards.subject: Defence in depth
says: layers several controls so one failure does not expose everything
assumes any single layer may be bypassed
cards.use: design protection that survives one control failing
not: relies on one very strong perimeter control

cards.subject: Zero trust
says: treats network location as no proof of trust
verifies every request regardless of where it originates
cards.use: stop assuming everything inside the office network is safe
not: trusts any request that arrives from the internal network

cards.subject: Risk
says: combines the likelihood of a threat with its impact
guides which threats to treat first
cards.use: need to rank which threat to fix first
not: is zero once a control exists

cards.subject: Spoofing
says: pretends to be another user or system
violates authentication
cards.use: see an attacker send requests as someone else
not: violates availability

cards.subject: Tampering
says: alters data or code without permission
violates integrity
cards.use: see an attacker modify a price in transit
not: violates confidentiality

cards.subject: Repudiation
says: lets someone deny an action when no reliable record exists
is countered by trustworthy audit logs
cards.use: hear a user claim they never approved a transfer
not: is an attacker reading data they should not

cards.subject: Information disclosure
says: exposes data to someone not authorised to see it
violates confidentiality
cards.use: find a verbose error leaking internal details
not: violates integrity

cards.subject: Denial of service
says: exhausts capacity so legitimate users cannot be served
violates availability
cards.use: see an attacker flood an endpoint until it stops responding
not: violates authorisation

cards.subject: Elevation of privilege
says: gains abilities beyond those granted
violates authorisation
cards.use: see a normal user reach an admin function
not: violates non-repudiation

cards.subject: Shifting left
says: moves security checks earlier in the lifecycle
makes flaws cheaper to fix
cards.use: want to find security flaws at design and coding time
not: delays security testing until after release

cards.subject: Secure code review
says: has a second person examine changes for security flaws
focuses on authentication, input handling and secrets
cards.use: want a human to spot logic flaws that scanners miss
not: is replaced entirely by a linter

cards.subject: Static application security testing
says: analyses source code without running it
can flag injection patterns early
produces false positives that need triage
cards.use: want automated scanning of code on every pull request
not: tests a running site from outside with no source access

cards.subject: Dynamic application security testing
says: tests a running application from the outside
finds runtime and configuration issues without seeing source lines
cards.use: want to probe a deployed staging site like an attacker
not: reads the source code for patterns

cards.subject: A penetration test
says: has skilled testers attempt to breach a system within an agreed scope
is a point-in-time assessment
cards.use: want an expert to try to break in under agreed rules
not: proves that no vulnerabilities remain

cards.subject: Fuzzing
says: feeds large volumes of malformed or random input to a program
finds crashes and parsing flaws
cards.use: want to stress a parser with unexpected input
not: reviews the design for threats

cards.subject: Security requirements
says: state the protections a feature must provide
are written before the design is settled
cards.use: begin a new feature that handles personal data
not: are added after the penetration test

cards.subject: Secure by default
says: ships with the safest settings enabled
makes users opt out of protection and not opt in
cards.use: choose the default value for a risky setting
not: ships with every feature enabled for convenience

cards.subject: A CVE identifier
says: is a public identifier for a specific known vulnerability
lets tools and teams refer to the same flaw
cards.use: need to look up a published flaw in a library
not: is a score from 0 to 10

cards.subject: A CVSS score
says: rates the technical severity of a vulnerability
does not by itself reflect your own business context
cards.use: need to rank vulnerabilities by severity before triage
not: identifies a vulnerability uniquely

cards.subject: A security regression test
says: keeps a fixed flaw from coming back
encodes the original exploit as an automated test
cards.use: have just fixed an access control bug
not: is run once by hand before release

cards.subject: Privacy by design
says: builds privacy protection into the design from the start
makes the privacy-friendly option the default
cards.use: plan a new feature that handles personal data
not: adds privacy notices after launch

cards.subject: Data minimisation
says: collects only what the purpose needs
reduces what a breach can expose
cards.use: decide which fields a signup form needs
not: collects everything in case it proves useful later

cards.subject: Purpose limitation
says: uses personal data only for the reasons stated when it was collected
requires a new basis before data is reused for a different purpose
cards.use: consider reusing support emails for marketing
not: permits any reuse as long as the data is stored securely

cards.subject: A retention limit
says: deletes data when it is no longer needed
is set deliberately for each type of data
cards.use: decide how long to keep old records
not: keeps data forever in case it is useful

cards.subject: Pseudonymisation
says: replaces identifiers with a token while the mapping is held separately
still counts as personal data because it can be reversed with the extra information
cards.use: want analysts to work with data without seeing names
not: makes re-identification impossible

cards.subject: Anonymisation
says: removes the link to a person irreversibly
is hard to achieve because combined fields can re-identify people
cards.use: want data to fall outside personal-data rules
not: is achieved by replacing a name with a user id

cards.subject: Personal data in URLs
says: ends up in browser history, proxy logs and server logs
is avoided by sending it in the request body
cards.use: consider putting an email address in a query string
not: is safe because HTTPS encrypts the URL in logs

cards.subject: GGLearn's password storage
says: stores values shaped scrypt$N$r$p$salt$hash
keeps the cost settings inside each stored hash
upgrades old salt:hash values the next time the person signs in
compares hashes with timingSafeEqual and hashes asynchronously
cards.use: need to know how GGLearn keeps a password
not: stores passwords encrypted so an admin can recover them

cards.subject: The GGLearn session cookie
says: holds the user id, issued-at time, version and an HMAC signature
is httpOnly, sameSite lax and secure in production
has its 30-day lifetime enforced by the server and not by the cookie expiry
cards.use: need to know what GGLearn puts in a session cookie
not: holds the user's password hash so the server can re-verify it

cards.subject: GGLearn's session_version
says: lets the server revoke every older session of a user at once
is used for Sign out everywhere and when someone is offboarded
cards.use: need to log a user out of all devices in GGLearn
not: makes logins faster

cards.subject: GGLearn's requireUser guard
says: re-reads the user from the database on each request
makes offboarding and role changes take effect immediately
cards.use: want a role change in GGLearn to apply without waiting for a new login
not: trusts the role stored inside the cookie

cards.subject: GGLearn's rank rule
says: stops a caller acting on someone of equal or higher rank
was added after a manager could offboard an admin
cards.use: see a GGLearn manager try to offboard an admin
not: lets a manager act on any user except themselves

cards.subject: The GGLearn drillCheck gap
says: returned the answer to any exam question for any signed-in user
was broken access control because enrolment and level were not checked
cards.use: recall the GGLearn flaw that could reveal exam answers
not: was a SQL injection in the login form

cards.subject: GGLearn's invite-only signup
says: replaced open self-signup
creates accounts through invite tokens at a join link
cards.use: learn how a new person gets a GGLearn account
not: lets anyone on the internet register

cards.subject: GGLearn's rate limiter
says: lives in process memory
assumes a single PM2 process
resets when the process restarts
cards.use: scale GGLearn to several processes and ask what breaks the login limit
not: is stored in a shared database table

cards.subject: TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS
says: sets how many hops from the end of X-Forwarded-For hold the client address
defaults to 2 behind Cloudflare and Apache
ignores anything a visitor added to the header
cards.use: need the real client address behind Cloudflare and Apache
not: takes the first entry of X-Forwarded-For as the client

cards.subject: GGLearn's Apache Cloudflare-only rule
says: restricts Apache to Cloudflare's published address ranges
stops direct requests that forge X-Forwarded-For
is regenerated by a script that refuses to write a suspicious address list
cards.use: want nobody to reach the origin without passing Cloudflare
not: is applied automatically as soon as the file exists, with no vhost change

cards.subject: ggmoney's Cloudflare SSL mode
says: is Full (strict)
avoids Flexible mode, which would send tokens unencrypted to the origin
cards.use: choose the Cloudflare SSL mode for ggmoney
not: is Flexible so that the origin needs no certificate

cards.subject: ggsocial's stored platform tokens
says: are encrypted with APP_SECRET
become unreadable if that key is lost
cards.use: ask what happens to saved platform tokens if APP_SECRET changes
not: are stored as plain text in the database

cards.subject: GGLearn's security headers
says: include HSTS, Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy
add a CSP covering frame, form, base-uri and object sources
switch off the X-Powered-By header
cards.use: check which browser protections GGLearn already sends
not: include a complete script-src CSP with nonces

cards.subject: GGLearn's open security items
says: include multi-factor authentication, which is not built
include a breached-password check left open by choice
include a full script-src CSP that needs nonces
cards.use: ask what the GGLearn review still lists as unfinished
not: have all been fixed in the latest review

qa.q: What is the main reason to store a salted slow hash of a password instead of the password itself?
qa.right: A leaked database does not directly reveal the passwords
wrong: It lets support staff read forgotten passwords
It makes the login page load faster
It removes the need for HTTPS
qa.why: A hash cannot be reversed, so a leak does not hand attackers the passwords.

qa.q: Where must an access control check be enforced to be trustworthy?
qa.right: On the server, for every sensitive request
wrong: In the browser, by hiding the button
qa.why: Anything in the client can be bypassed by calling the server directly.

qa.q: Which of these is the strongest primary defence against SQL injection?
qa.right: Parameterised queries
wrong: Making the database port private only
qa.why: Separating SQL from data stops data being parsed as code.

qa.q: Why should secrets not be committed to source control?
qa.right: History keeps them even after the file is deleted, and many people can read the repository
wrong: Git cannot store text with symbols
Secrets are only valid for one commit
qa.why: A committed secret must be treated as leaked.

qa.q: Which cookie flag stops page JavaScript from reading a session cookie?
qa.right: HttpOnly
qa.why: HttpOnly hides the cookie from scripts; Secure restricts it to HTTPS.

qa.q: A teammate says Base64-encoding a token makes it safe to put in a public URL. What is the problem?
qa.right: Base64 is a reversible encoding, so it hides nothing
wrong: Base64 output is too long for URLs
qa.why: Anyone can decode it with no key.

qa.q: What should a login error message say when the password is wrong?
qa.right: A generic message that does not reveal whether the email exists
wrong: Tell the user the email is not registered
Tell the user which characters were correct
Include the database error to help debugging
qa.why: Different messages allow account enumeration.

qa.q: What is the purpose of an audit log?
qa.right: To record who did what, to which target and when, for sensitive actions
wrong: To store application passwords for recovery
qa.why: Audit logs give accountability and support investigation.

qa.q: Which is a sound reason to keep dependency versions pinned in a lockfile?
qa.right: Builds are repeatable and an unexpected new version cannot slip in silently
wrong: It guarantees the dependencies have no vulnerabilities
It removes the need to update them
qa.why: Pinning gives repeatability, not safety; you still need to update deliberately.

qa.q: A JWT is signed with HS256 and stored in localStorage with a 30-day expiry. A user's device is stolen. What is the real limitation?
qa.right: The server cannot revoke the token before expiry without keeping extra state
wrong: The signature stops working after the device is stolen
JWTs cannot be sent over HTTPS
The payload is encrypted so it cannot be inspected
qa.why: Stateless tokens need a revocation mechanism such as a version or deny list.

qa.q: Why is CORS not an access control mechanism?
qa.right: The browser enforces it, so non-browser clients ignore it
wrong: It only works for GET requests
qa.why: CORS relaxes a browser rule; the server still has to authorise each request.

qa.q: A search page shows the query back to the user inside the HTML. Which fix is most appropriate?
qa.right: Encode the output for the HTML context
wrong: Strip the word script from the input
Convert the query to lower case
qa.why: Context-aware output encoding is the main XSS defence.

qa.q: What does SSRF let an attacker do?
qa.right: Make the server request a URL of the attacker's choosing, such as an internal service
wrong: Run script in another user's browser
qa.why: The server's network position becomes the attacker's.

qa.q: Which design choice best limits SSRF risk in a feature that fetches a user-supplied URL?
qa.right: Allow-list the destinations and block private and metadata address ranges
wrong: Fetch the URL from the browser and not the server
Only check the URL ends in .com
qa.why: Deny lists and string checks are easy to bypass; allow-listing is stronger.

qa.q: What does STRIDE stand for in threat modelling?
qa.right: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege
wrong: Secrets, Tokens, Roles, Injection, Defaults, Encryption
Scanning, Testing, Review, Isolation, Detection, Escalation
Sessions, Transport, Rotation, Integrity, Disclosure, Exposure
qa.why: It is a category checklist applied to a data flow diagram.

qa.q: Why can a successful password reset email flow become an account takeover path?
qa.right: Whoever controls the mailbox or can guess or reuse the reset token controls the account
wrong: Reset emails are never encrypted by TLS
Resetting always deletes the old password hash
qa.why: Reset tokens must be random, single-use and short-lived.

qa.q: Why should a login handler compare a submitted token with the expected one using a constant-time function?
qa.right: Ordinary comparison can leak how many leading characters matched through timing
wrong: It stops the token being logged
qa.why: Timing differences can be measured and used to recover secrets.

qa.q: Why is ECB mode a poor choice for encrypting structured data?
qa.right: Identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks, which reveals patterns
qa.why: Use an authenticated mode such as GCM with a unique nonce.

qa.q: What goes wrong when AES-GCM reuses a nonce under the same key?
qa.right: Confidentiality and authentication can both be broken
wrong: Nothing; the nonce is only decorative
qa.why: A unique nonce per encryption is a hard requirement.

qa.q: Why does PKCE help a mobile app using the authorisation code flow?
qa.right: An intercepted authorisation code cannot be redeemed without the secret the app created
wrong: It removes the need for TLS
It extends the access token lifetime
qa.why: PKCE ties the code exchange to the client that started it.

qa.q: A coupon endpoint checks the coupon is unused, then marks it used in a separate step. What attack does this invite?
qa.right: A race condition, where two parallel requests both pass the check
qa.why: Make the check and the update one atomic operation.

qa.q: What does a Content Security Policy chiefly add?
qa.right: A browser-side limit on where scripts and content may load from, reducing XSS damage
qa.why: CSP is defence in depth, not a replacement for encoding.

qa.q: Why is a per-IP login limit alone not enough against a botnet?
qa.right: The attack is spread across many addresses, so each stays under the limit
wrong: Limits only work on GET requests
qa.why: Also limit per account and watch for patterns.

qa.q: Which is the best fix for a production API key found in an old commit?
qa.right: Revoke and replace the key, then investigate use, and scrub history as a secondary step
wrong: Delete the file in a new commit
qa.why: The secret is compromised once exposed; removal alone does not undo that.

qa.q: What attack does JWT algorithm confusion exploit?
qa.right: A verifier that trusts the algorithm named in the token header, such as accepting none
wrong: A server that stores tokens in cookies
A token that expires too soon
A client that sends tokens over HTTP
qa.why: The server must fix the accepted algorithms itself.

qa.q: What does envelope encryption let you do that single-key encryption does not?
qa.right: Rotate the master key by re-wrapping data keys without re-encrypting all the data
wrong: Use the same key for every customer safely
qa.why: Data keys are encrypted under the master key.

qa.q: Why can anonymisation be harder than it looks?
qa.right: Combinations of ordinary fields such as postcode, birth date and sex can re-identify people
wrong: Names cannot be removed from databases
qa.why: Quasi-identifiers combine into unique fingerprints.

qa.q: What makes a dependency confusion attack possible?
qa.right: A build tool preferring a public package over an internal one with the same name
wrong: A package with a typo in its name
qa.why: Scoped names and registry pinning prevent it.

qa.q: Why pin a CI action to a full commit hash rather than a tag?
qa.right: A tag can be moved to different code, while a hash cannot
wrong: Tags are not supported in CI
qa.why: Pinning protects against a moved or hijacked tag.

qa.q: What is wrong with this query?
qa.right: It builds SQL by joining user input, which allows SQL injection
wrong: It compares email with an equals sign
qa.why: Use a placeholder and pass the value separately.
qa.code:
const sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + req.body.email + "'";
db.query(sql);

qa.q: Which change fixes the injection safely?
qa.right: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1", [email])
wrong: db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email.replace("'", "") + "'")
db.query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email.toLowerCase() + "'")
qa.why: Placeholders separate code from data; quote stripping is bypassable.

qa.q: What is the vulnerability in this route?
qa.right: Any signed-in user can read any invoice by changing the id, because ownership is not checked
qa.why: Add a check that the invoice belongs to the caller.

qa.q: What risk does this code carry?
qa.right: The user-controlled name can contain ../ and read files outside the uploads folder
wrong: The file may be too large
The response lacks a status code
qa.why: Resolve the path and confirm it stays inside the base directory.

qa.q: What is the most serious problem here?
qa.right: The host is concatenated into a shell command, enabling command injection
wrong: The callback has no error handling
exec is deprecated in all languages
qa.why: Avoid the shell and validate the host against a strict format.

qa.q: What does this code allow an attacker to do?
qa.right: Set their own role (for example admin) by adding it to the request body
qa.why: Pick the allowed fields explicitly instead of passing the whole body.

qa.q: Why is this password storage insecure?
qa.right: SHA-256 is fast and unsalted, so stolen hashes can be cracked at scale
wrong: SHA-256 cannot be computed in Node
qa.why: Use a salted, slow algorithm such as scrypt, bcrypt or Argon2.
qa.code:
const hash = crypto.createHash("sha256").update(password).digest("hex");
await db.users.insert({ email, hash });

qa.q: Why is this reset token generation weak?
qa.right: Math.random is not cryptographically secure, so tokens can be predicted
qa.why: Use crypto.randomBytes or an equivalent secure generator.
qa.code:
const token = Math.random().toString(36).slice(2);
await saveResetToken(user.id, token);

qa.q: What does this redirect handler allow?
qa.right: An open redirect, sending victims from a trusted domain to an attacker's site
qa.why: Only redirect to relative paths or an allow-list of destinations.

qa.q: Which cookie flags are missing from this session cookie?
qa.right: HttpOnly, Secure and a SameSite attribute
qa.why: Set all three so scripts, plain HTTP and cross-site sends are limited.

qa.q: What is the risk in this front-end code?
qa.right: Untrusted data is written as HTML, enabling DOM-based XSS
qa.why: Use textContent or encode before inserting.

qa.q: What is the risk when a logger writes this line?
qa.right: The credential ends up in the log files
qa.why: Log the event and the user id; never passwords or tokens.

qa.q: Why is this fetch endpoint dangerous?
qa.right: It requests any URL the caller gives, including internal addresses, which is SSRF
wrong: It returns text instead of JSON
qa.why: Allow-list destinations and block private ranges.

qa.q: What does this Python code expose?
qa.right: Remote code execution, since unpickling untrusted data can run attacker-chosen code
qa.why: Never deserialise untrusted data with pickle; use a data-only format.

qa.q: What is the flaw in this CORS configuration?
qa.right: Reflecting any origin while allowing credentials lets any site read authenticated responses
qa.why: Allow only named trusted origins when credentials are involved.

qa.q: What is the risk in how this token is checked?
qa.right: String comparison can leak timing information about the expected token
wrong: The token is compared as a number
qa.why: Use a constant-time comparison such as crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length buffers.

qa.q: What is the flaw in using jwt.decode for authentication here?
qa.right: decode does not verify the signature, so a forged token is accepted
qa.why: Use verify with a fixed algorithm and key.

qa.q: A team is adding a feature that lets users upload profile photos. What should they do first?
qa.right: Validate type and size on the server, store files outside the web root under generated names
wrong: Trust the file extension the browser sends
Store files in the web root under their original names
Accept any type to avoid user complaints
qa.why: Original names and extensions invite path and execution problems.

qa.q: A developer says client-side form validation is enough. What is the best reply?
qa.right: Validate on the server too, because requests can bypass the browser
wrong: Agree; the browser is the trusted tool
Move validation to a CSS rule
qa.why: Client checks are for usability, not security.

qa.q: Logins start succeeding from many accounts with valid password pairs, each account tried once from different IPs. What is most likely happening?
qa.right: Credential stuffing using pairs leaked from another service
qa.why: Reused passwords and one attempt per account fit credential stuffing.

qa.q: A manager can promote anyone to admin through a form field the server accepts as-is. Which control would have prevented this?
qa.right: Server-side checks that the caller outranks the target and may set that role
wrong: Hiding the field in the form
Making the field read-only in CSS
qa.why: Role changes must be authorised on the server.

qa.q: A security scanner reports 200 findings on the first run. What is the best way to start?
qa.right: Triage by exposure and impact, fix the highest risks first, and tune out false positives
wrong: Treat every finding as critical and stop releases
qa.why: Triage by real risk avoids both paralysis and neglect.

qa.q: A developer wants to store API keys in the frontend config because the app is private. What is the best advice?
qa.right: Keep keys on the server; anything shipped to the browser is readable by any user
qa.why: A secret in a client bundle is not a secret.

qa.q: A shared service account has been used by five teams and its key has leaked. What should happen first?
qa.right: Rotate the key and issue separate least-privilege credentials per team
wrong: Wait to see if the key is misused
Delete the logs to avoid confusion
Share the new key in chat
qa.why: Containment first, then reduce sharing.

qa.q: A user says they never approved a payment and the system has no record of who clicked. Which STRIDE category is the gap?
qa.right: Repudiation
qa.why: Without trustworthy audit logs, actions can be denied.

qa.q: After a bug fix, the same access control flaw returns three releases later. What would best prevent a repeat?
qa.right: An automated regression test that reproduces the original exploit
qa.why: Tests make a fix durable.

qa.q: A team puts a rate limit in application memory and then scales to four processes. What happens to the limit?
qa.right: Each process counts separately, so the effective limit is roughly four times higher
wrong: Nothing changes because counters are shared automatically
qa.why: In-memory state is per process; use shared storage for multi-process limits.

qa.q: An app trusts the first entry of X-Forwarded-For for rate limiting. Why is that unsafe?
qa.right: A client can send its own value, which proxies append to, so the attacker controls the first entry
wrong: The first entry is always the proxy
The header is only sent on POST
qa.why: Count trusted hops from the end of the chain.

qa.q: A team enables a strict CSP but still uses inline event handlers. What is the likely outcome?
qa.right: The inline handlers are blocked unless the policy allows them, so features break
qa.why: A strict script-src needs nonces or hashes and no inline handlers.
